messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Latexdiff
messages.body_plain:
On Sunday, September 30, 2012 1:22:18 AM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> Perhaps the most promising git-centric wrapper around latexdiff seems to be
>
> https://gitorious.org/git-latexdiff
>
> However, latexdiff was not particularly close to generating a useful (and syntactically correct) .tex file with the differences in the manual for v1.0.2 relative to v1.0.1 . I started to manually fix the latex errors but gave up after fixing about half of them. In particular, it has problems with \Verb and some with displaymath.
>
> This might get easier in the future when there are a smaller number of changes to the manual, but it looks like it will never be fully automatic.
>
> Ben

OK, I will probably regret saying this, but we could (in principle) write our own script to use instead of latexdiff (which was written well before git existed).

First, the on-screen output of

git diff --unified=0 --inter-hunk-context=0 --word-diff --color=always v1.0.1 v1.0.2 src/docs/stan-reference/

is pretty useful and is probably adequate for people to skim as long as they can compile latex in their head. The arguments

--unified=0 prints 0 lines of context
--inter-hunk-context=0 similar to --unified=0
--word-diff looks for changes by "word" (which basically means delimited by whitespace)
--color=always makes additions show up in green and deletions in red
v1.0.1 v1.0.2 means between these two tags
src/docs/stan-reference/ means everything in that directory

In practice, the unwritten script would probably process one .tex file at a time.

I am attaching the output of the above as all_changes.txt in case you don't have git readily available. You loose the coloration but you can still see additions, which are enclosed by {+ and +} and deletions, which are enclosed by [- and -].

What we want to do is temporarily add markers to the .tex files so that they will indicate what has been added (and possibly deleted) and then compile a temporary version of the manual that has the changes highlighted. This is pretty straightforward for the case where whole lines have been added since v1.0.1 . Using the example of acknowledgements.tex, this opqaque command

git diff --unified=0 --inter-hunk-context=0 --word-diff --color=never v1.0.1 v1.0.2 src/docs/stan-reference/acknowledgements.tex | grep ^\{+.*+}$ | sed 's/{+%+}//' | sed '/\\.*{.*}.*+}$/ d' | sed 's/^{+/s\//' | sed 's/+}$/\/\\\\A{\&}\//' > /tmp/sedscript.sh

yields a sedscript.sh file with these lines

s/Thanks to Jeffrey Arnold for submitting code patches and reporting/\\A{&}/
s/a whole bunch of bugs for earlier versions. /\\A{&}/
s/Thanks to Jeffrey Arnold, Eric N.~Brown, and Wayne Folta for/\\A{&}/
s/submitting documentation patches./\\A{&}/
s/We're really thankful to everyone who's had the patience to try/\\A{&}/
s/to get Stan working and reported bugs.  All the gory details are/\\A{&}/
s/available from Stan's issue tracker at the following URL./\\A{&}/

where the & basically means "substitute the thing between the preceding / / here". Then

sed -i -f /tmp/sedscript.sh src/docs/stan-reference/acknowledgements.tex

changes the existing acknowledgements.tex file so it now has lines like

\subsection*{Code  and Doc Patches}

\A{Thanks to Jeffrey Arnold for submitting code patches and reporting}
\A{a whole bunch of bugs for earlier versions. }

\A{Thanks to Jeffrey Arnold, Eric N.~Brown, and Wayne Folta for}
\A{submitting documentation patches.}

\subsection*{Bug Reports}

\A{We're really thankful to everyone who's had the patience to try}
\A{to get Stan working and reported bugs.  All the gory details are}
\A{available from Stan's issue tracker at the following URL.}

Thus, if we define the \A{} macro with a \newcommand to be green text or underlined or something and compile, then the parts in the acknowledgments section added before v1.0.2 was tagged would be highlighted accordingly in the PDF.

And then we do

git reset --hard HEAD

and it's as if nothing ever happened to acknowledgements.tex in master.

Maybe that is already enough, but we could also handle intra-line edits in a roughly similar fashion. So, the question becomes is it worth making such a script and robustifying it?

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Rcpp 0.9.14 & clang++ 3.1?
messages.body_plain:
I made a diff between Rcpp 0.9.14 and 0.9.13, which tells me
essentially nothing related really changed.  Then I did not
understand what Dirk said regarding clang.  But who cares.
So the bottom line is that the new version would not have any
new impact on RStan.

RStan allow those users who know how to change the c++ compiler to
change that just as those compiler flags.  In essential, RStan do not
control what compiler is used, it just use package inline, which calls
`R CMD SHLIB`.  R CMD SHLIB will call GNU make, which will
use whatever is configure in those Makevars files at different places.

I guess there is/was some problem with Rcpp (current version
and previous version) if clang++ (version before 3.1?).

--
Jiqiang

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Latexdiff
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, October 1, 2012 2:17:13 AM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> OK, I will probably regret saying this, but we could (in principle) write our own script to use instead of latexdiff (which was written well before git existed).

Doing this is somewhat annoying, but it is manageable. This script I wrote

#!/bin/bash -e

OLD_VERSION=$1
NEW_VERSION=$2

ADDED_LINE=^\{+.*+}$
IGNORE_COMMENT_LINE='/{+%\s*+}/d'
IGNORE_LINE_WITH_LEADING_SLASH='/^{+\\/d'
IGNORE_LATEX_MACROS='/\\[A-Za-z]*{.*}/d'
IGNORE_ALL_BRACES='/^{+.*[{}].*+}$/d'
FIX_COMMENTS='s@%@}@'
ESCAPE_SLASH='s@\\@\\\\@'
ESCAPE_AMPERSAND='s@\&@\\\&@'
ESCAPE_AT='s@\@@\\\@@'
ESCAPE_BRACKET='s@\[@\\\[@'
DELETE_BRACEPLUS='s@^{+@s\@\^@'
ADD_MACRO='s@+}$@\$\@\\\\A{\&}\@@'

TEX_FILES=`ls *.tex`
for TEX_FILE in $TEX_FILES; do
        if [ "stan-reference.tex" = "$TEX_FILE" ]; then
                continue
        fi
        git diff --unified=0 --inter-hunk-context=0 --word-diff --color=never $OLD_VERSION $NEW_VERSION $TEX_FILE | \
        grep ${ADDED_LINE} | \
        sed ${IGNORE_LINE_WITH_LEADING_SLASH} | \
        sed ${IGNORE_COMMENT_LINE} | \
#       sed ${IGNORE_LATEX_MACROS} | \
        sed ${IGNORE_ALL_BRACES} | \
        sed ${FIX_COMMENTS} | \
        sed ${ESCAPE_SLASH} | \
        sed ${ESCAPE_AMPERSAND} | \
        sed ${ESCAPE_AT} | \
        sed ${ESCAPE_BRACKET} | \
        sed ${DELETE_BRACEPLUS} | \
        sed ${ADD_MACRO} > \
        sedscript.sh
        echo 'Processing ' $TEX_FILE
        sed -i -f sedscript.sh $TEX_FILE
        rm sedscript.sh
done

essentially puts (most) lines that were added between v1.0.1 and v1.0.2 within a \A{} macro and I have for now done \newcommand{\A}{\textcolor{green}} although we could do something else to be better for colorblind people. The attached PDF manual has this done for the Appendices only (starting at p.183).

The main annoying thing is our frequent use of the Verbatim environment. Thus, something like

\begin{Verbatim}
model {
  \A{real x;}
}
\end{Verbatim}

comes out literally instead of just putting real x; in green. We can get around this by using the alltt package / environment in these situations, which is like Verbatim in terms of spacing but processes interior macros. The annoying thing with that is that you have to escape the braces to get them to compile as braces, so this works:

\begin{alltt}
model \{
  \A{real x;}
\}
\end{alltt}

I didn't go though and escape every brace in the Appendices though, so some things are a little off. Also, it is a bit hit-and-miss with what it currently makes green because I was conservative in only processing lines that would (probably) not break the compilation (too badly). But that could probably be improved as well as processing in-line edits in addition to entirely new lines.

So, my question basically is do people have opinions as to whether this is worth regularly doing for the whole reference manual?

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Done. So, if you find yourself responding to a common problem on stan-users (forgetting to constrain a variable, looping instead of vectorizing, trying to sample integer parameters, etc.) it would be better to post under the FAQ thread

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/4gv3fNCqSNk/X95DtUBCGCwJ

Be sure to change the subject and make the first sentence of your reply descriptive of the problem. Then reply to the OP and include a link to your response on the FAQ thread. You can find this link in the Google Groups interface but clicking on the drop-down box that says "Post reply" and selecting "Link". Conversely, it would probably be good to link to the OP's thread at the end of your response on the FAQ thread.

Also, the first four posts on the FAQ thread give instructions for dealing with parser / compiler / runtime / rstan errors so when someone says "Stan is not working!!!" but doesn't provide the necessary information to fix the problem, refer them to the appropriate direct link.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
On 10/4/12 10:15 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> RE: mixing types
>
> This guy seems to have had some success hacking mixed types with a different auto-diff library
>
> http://listengine.tuxfamily.org/lists.tuxfamily.org/eigen/2012/10/msg00018.html

Too bad it's only a sketchy note and apparently makes
as much use of C++11 as possible.  Note the discussion that
follows on temporaries -- that's my main concern at this
point, because if we don't solve it, there's nothing to
gain for Stan in either expressiveness or speed.

> As I recall, I got multiplication between mixed types to work by tricking Eigen into thinking everything was a double
> and Marcus did something with traits that used less trickery. But I think we couldn't do mixed type addition, which is
> what that guy got working with a functor. Maybe we could try again? I git pulled master into the mixed_types branch on
> Google a few days ago, which was giant but only had a couple of trivial merger conflicts.

I'd love to get this sorted out.

If we want to have the benefit of expression templates,
then I want to say again that we need to either

a) pull out proper binary traits for binary ops throughout
    Eigen, OR

b) follow their type-specific hack for std::complex, only
    with more thoroughness;  their std::complex hack doesn't
    work with all the solvers and doesn't even cover both
    orders of multiplication if memory servers.

Just writing operator* for Matrix isn't enough -- we need
to handle all of the expression templates, or it doesn't
buy us anything.  (That is, our solution can't just convert
everything to Matrix, or we lose the no-intermediate-struct
benefit of the expression templates.)  Specifically, we need
to roll in our own customized implementations of product
as Marcus did in agrad/matrix.

I never got close to doing that when I tried the
operator*() specialization route.  I'll have to take
a look at what Ben did.  (After learning a bit more
about how git deals with branches, which I've been
meaning to do for ages.)

> RE: Jeigen
>
> Another guy made a Java wrapper for Eigen
>
> https://github.com/hughperkins/jeigen
>
> So, Bob can probably make JavaStan in about 10 minutes.

I'm sure I could do it, but I don't see the point.
We can't really expose much of the API through Java,
and if we just want to run models, there's the command line.

- Bob

DoubleMatrix.cast(var) * SameVarMatrix + SameVarMatrix;

and maybe his workaround for that involved C++11. But, off the top of my head, it seems like there is a lot more of the first construction in Stan and not much of the second.

messages.subject: ccache
messages.body_plain:
Today I just discovered ccache

https://ccache.samba.org/

and would recommend it to anyone who tracks the git repository (including Jenkins, if we can get ccache working on 64-bit Windows). Essentially, it caches compilations so that they can be reused if the file doesn't change (even if you do make clean-all beforehand).

After installing and configuring, run it once serially so that it can cache Stan's C++ files

goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ make clean-all && time make CC="ccache g++" O=3 test-models > /tmp/g++_caching.log
...
real    93m52.243s
user    87m29.122s
sys     4m58.650s

Now files are cached:
goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ ccache -s
cache directory                     /home/goodrich/.ccache
cache hit (direct)                     0
cache hit (preprocessed)               0
cache miss                           158
called for link                      147
unsupported compiler option           11
files in cache                       464
cache size                         163.3 Mbytes
max cache size                       1.0 Gbytes

Now, you can henceforth do it in parallel much faster and with much more limited RAM spikes
goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ make clean-all && time make CC="ccache g++" O=3 -j8 test-models > /tmp/g++_cached.log
...
real    11m48.354s
user    58m20.964s
sys     2m42.890s

goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ ccache -s
cache directory                     /home/goodrich/.ccache
cache hit (direct)                   145
cache hit (preprocessed)               8
cache miss                           163
called for link                      294
unsupported compiler option          417
files in cache                       456
cache size                         159.2 Mbytes
max cache size                       1.0 Gbytes

We can save a couple more minutes once I make an unrelated tweak to the lsat test. But it already takes only half the time as a parallel run without caching
goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ make clean-all && time make CC=g++ O=3 -j8 test-models > /tmp/g++_nocached.log
...
real    23m3.460s
user    140m26.479s
sys     4m8.016s

I don't think ccache works properly with clang++ yet, but clang++ is already decently fast on test-models.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ccache
messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, October 6, 2012 1:17:32 PM UTC-4, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> I used the tempfile() to overcome a problem in Rcpp, which seems do not allow me use the same name in different shared libraries.  So ideally I want that name to be unique.

Right. It would definitely be bad to have multiple shared libraries trying to call anon_model. But the question becomes can we largely avoid that in a more flexible manner. Maybe making the default model_name be paste0("anon_model_", tempfile()) and using the model_name for the class? I guess that is a problem if users want to have two models called "rats" in the same R session, but it seems like we could just require them to use different names.

> But the issue here is the another tempfile() gets called by package inline to create the temporary cpp file to be compiled using R CMD SHLIB.

As far as I understand, that is not actually a problem because ccache matches on the file hash rather than the file name. So inline can randomly name the .cpp file whatever it wants, and it will still have the same hash unless the source has been changed.

messages.body_plain:
On 10/8/12 4:27 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Friday, October 5, 2012 6:21:17 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:

> So, if it is the case that ||b.cast<var>()|| does not make a temporary, as suggested by the (rather minimal)
> documentation at
>
> http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/classEigen_1_1MatrixBase.html#a660200abaf1fc4b888330a37d6132b76

> which does say that the result is an expression, then do we really need so much specialized promotion / to_var()
> business  that interferes with writing regular Eigen code?

 From what I can tell from a brief dip into the Eigen
code, the doc's right -- it creates a templated view of
the underlying matrix.

The problem is later, when you access elements.  There
they'll get cast on an access-by-access basis, which is
even worse!  This creates a new auto-dif var on the stack
for every access, not just for every double matrix.

Finally, what we really need is to create our own
expression templates that would use implementations of
the basic multiply, etc. ops like the ones Marcus has
coded in stan/agrad/matrix.

> Is the answer that the above wastes a small amount of time
> calculating dc/db00 and dc/db10 and if so, can we do something about that? Or is the answer that we would have to write
> an equally frustrating amount of code in order to test whether we need to do a .cast<var>() ?

 > I assume (perhaps wrongly)
> that if b were already a Matrix<var,Dynamic,Dynamic> then ||b.cast<var>() ||would be a no-op, so can we just cast
> everywhere but the double op double case?

That should be right -- casts of type T to type T
should be compilable away because the types of everything
are known at compile time.  But see above.

Overall, what I think we need to do is either

A)  upgrade all their unary trait specifications to
     ternary (operand1, operand2, result),

OR

B)  follow their complex implementation.

For instance, in option (B), here's what they do for op casts
lib/eigen_3.1.1/Eigen//src/plugins/CommonCwiseUnaryOps.h:

   /** Overloaded for efficient real matrix times complex scalar value */
   inline const CwiseUnaryOp<internal::scalar_multiple2_op<Scalar,std::complex<Scalar> >, const Derived>
   operator*(const std::complex<Scalar>& scalar) const
   {
     return CwiseUnaryOp<internal::scalar_multiple2_op<Scalar,std::complex<Scalar> >, const Derived>
       (*static_cast<const Derived*>(this), internal::scalar_multiple2_op<Scalar,std::complex<Scalar> >(scalar));
   }

The problem for us [in addition to fueling Michael B's
faith in this wasteful paren style :-)] is that we need to go
one step further for efficiency.  We need to override not
just the scalar ops, but the ops at matrix levels so we can
have efficient derivatives.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: missing data
messages.body_plain:
On 10/8/12 1:33 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
 > Now that Eigen has essentially full support for sparse matrices,
 > can we revisit this idea for dealing with an arbitrary
 > missingness pattern in the data?

Sure -- it's just a matter of prioritizing what you're
intersted in doing.  All of the things you've put on the table
would be good for Stan:

   -- caching covariance data structure
   -- LKJ gradients
   -- basic Eigen operator traits and expression templates
   -- missing data with sparsity hack
   -- sparse vectors

   -- auto-dif unfolds for linear algebra (that may be me, not you)

Other than the LKJ gradients and auto-dif unfolds for
linear algebra, they're all fairly substantial projects
that involve the guts of Stan's parsing, data/param I/O, and
type inference (assignment, sampling, function calls, operators).

The really big change for the sparsity solution with mirrors would
be handling NA somehow (that's a very fundamental change) and
a whole bunch of I/O and type inference if the mirror solution can't
be reduced to a regular matrix op, which it can't be efficiently.

- Bob

>     Overall, what I think we need to do is either
>
>     A)  upgrade all their unary trait specifications to
>           ternary (operand1, operand2, result),
>
>     OR
>
>     B)  follow their complex implementation.
>
>
> I still like C) cheat, although A) probably would create the most value for Eigen. But since traits-related stuff is
> defined and used throughout the Eigen tree, it is hard for me to grasp all the places where we would need to ternarize.

I've said this before, but I think the way we're
cheating now is more effective speed wise than the
ways you suggest.  The point is that if we can partially
evaluate the auto-difs for an operation like matrix
multiply, it's a huge saving.  In fact, it's a much bigger
saving than we'd get from the Eigen expression templates,
which still unfold into basic ops.

I agree (A) would create value for Eigen.  The problem with
(B) is that we'd almost certainly have to branch, which is
highly undesirable.

I fear that unless we combine (A) and (B), it won't even be
as efficient as what we have now.

Once we partial eval gradients for things like inverse and
determinant (I don't know about the solvers), a lot of the
motivation for (A) and (B) go away.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: missing data
messages.body_plain:
On Monday, October 8, 2012 2:17:41 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> The really big change for the sparsity solution with mirrors would
> be handling NA somehow (that's a very fundamental change) and
> a whole bunch of I/O and type inference if the mirror solution can't
> be reduced to a regular matrix op, which it can't be efficiently.

I understand that it would be a big undertaking, but I'm not sure I understand what you are saying here. Under my proposal, the user would have to shift the observed data so that none were zero, recode the NAs as zeros, and somehow indicate in the .stan file that the matrix should have sparse storage. I don't think we would need to directly handle the NAs as special values like R does.

For the X_mirror sparse matrix of missing-values-as-parameters, the basics of what we need are

-- a way to construct / fill it
-- X_mirror * coefficients
-- row(X_mirror, i)
-- col(X_mirror, j)
-- X_mirror(i,j)

and Eigen has all of those now (although X_mirror(i,j) is slow). But users would probably be doing things like

col(X_mirror,j) ~ normal(mu, sigma);

so, we would also have to overload the densities to ignore the zeros in the sparse vector.

There are probably other things that we will need, but there are not that many operations that I would expect to be used on X_mirror if sparse matrices were only being used for missing data. If we also wanted to have sparse covariance matrices and whatnot, then we would have to implement a lot more, but that could wait.

But, since it is a big undertaking no matter what, does anyone have other ideas for a convenient way for users to handle arbitrary missingness patterns?

Ben

Inside R, we know the (maximum) length of the stuff being passed in the data list. So, stan() could just glue a #define on top of the .cpp file after stanc makes it but before it is compiled.

> > I don't know what exactly the stochastic differential equation guy had in mind, but here is a simple but unlikely
> > example. Suppose you have a parameter alpha, and you need a transformed parameter beta that goes into the likelihood.
> > And you know that

> be some probability distribution or something that
> would need this.  Is there a simple applied example

Actually, there are probability distributions that need implicit differentiation but that would usually entail us writing C++ rather than getting it from the user. There are many distributions where the quantile function (inverse of CDF) is known in closed form, but the PDF (and CDF) are not known in closed form. For example,

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tukey_lambda_distribution

The deal with these things is that you can explicitly write the density in terms of the quantile (the proportion of the mass to the left of x) but not in terms of x. So, given x, you have to numerically solve for the corresponding quantile and then evaluate the density. And then, in the HMC context, get the right gradient because the quantile that is a root of the implicit function is in turn a function of the unknown parameters.

This is actually an area where Stan could make a big contribution. These distributions that are defined by quantile functions are very flexible, but they don't get used much in the literature because the density is not available in the closed form. So, calculating the MLEs is hard, and doing Gibbs sampling is impossible.

> > Maybe more relevant, eigenvalues can be seen as the roots of det(Sigma - lambda * I) = 0, and so you can use the
> > gradient of lambda with respect to the parameters that generated Sigma to circumvent a ton of auto-diff.
>
> I'll have to think about that one.  I didn't see anythning
> to do with eigenvalues analytically in the Matrix Cookbook,
> but I should look at Magnus and Neudecker, too.

The eigenvalues are not known analytically; the derivatives of the eigenvalues with respect to the parameters are known analytically (but are a function of the eigenvectors). Here is a reference

http://gifi.stat.ucla.edu/janspubs/2007/reports/deleeuw_R_07c.pdf

Ben

> > rstan does not use R's pseduo random number generators; rather Stan's uses one of Boost's PRNGs. I'm still not convinced

> Optimal in what sense?  It's very easy to change.

The main criteria that I see experts talking about are the entropy, the speed, and the reproducibility. What rstan is doing now is probably not optimal with respect to any of these because it feeds in a pseudo-random seed by default.

> I should explain what we're doing more clearly in
> the manual.  I plugged in the L'Ecuyer RNG with
> a seed for chain 1.  Then each subsequent chain
> uses skip-ahead so the random numbers don't clash.
> I used a very very large skip ahead that would
> require a whole lot of random numbers per chain.
> I'll look it up and put the right numbers in.

This is what is confusing to me. The guy has written multiple PRNGs. The manual refers to a 1999 paper that does have some good properties when used in parallel, but the Boost code refers to a 1988 paper.

> The period of L'Ecuyer is pretty good, but
> speed isn't optimal.  And if you do things like
> use consecutive or close seeds, you get closely
> related random numbers at least initially.
>
> The C++ code lets you plug and play Boost RNGs
> (or other RNGs implementing their concept.)

Because I don't understand this stuff well, I would feel better if we used something from

http://trng.berlios.de/

as the PRNG. It is BSD, it is small, it is designed to be like Boost, it formed the basis for a proposal to get it into the C++11 standard, and the designers have explicitly thought about parallelism. So, to me, it is worth another dependency.

Ben

      if (!check_not_nan(function, y, "Random variable", &logp, Policy()))

template <class T>

so it seems to me that we can avoid calling check_not_nan(). I guess the exception message will be slightly less clear

" is %1%, but must be finite!"

when %1% evaluates to nan but  that is a small price to pay to avoid an extra sweep over the values every time the function is called.

messages.body_plain:
On Sat, Oct 13, 2012 at 6:22 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> There are a ton of them in Stan :) . I have long thought that there was a problem with many of them, and that they could be replaced by Eigen's template expressions (unless they involve mixed operations or special cases relating to auto-diff). I pointed this out to Bob many months ago, and he claimed that the C-style for loops were essentially what the compiler would produce for the equivalent Eigen template expression. But, from my (limited) understanding of
>
> http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/TopicInsideEigenExample.html
>
> this is not correct.
>
> They go into exhaustive detail about how Eigen (can) take aligned floating-point numbers and loop over packets of 4 values, rather than values. In particular, to add vectors v and w of length 50 (4 * 12 + 2) and assign them to the vector u, their expression templates ultimately yield code like
>
>   for(int i = 0; i < 4*(size/4); i+=4) u.packet(i)  = v.packet(i) + w.packet(i);
>
>   for(int i = 4*(size/4); i < size; i++) u[i] = v[i] + w[i];
>
>
> which is almost 4 times faster than
>
>   for(int i = 0; i < size; i++) u[i] = v[i] + w[i];
>

This is a result of explicitly using SIMD operations (implied by the packet(i) calls) which can be ~ 2-4 times faster for an operation like that.  Note however that SIMD instructions only work for basic types, namely float and double.  There is little to be done easily to exploit SIMD instructions for operations on var types.

> But in Stan, there are many places where we are "Doing the C Thing" instead of "Doing the Eigen Thing". To take a simple example, starting at line 1007 of src/stan/math/matrix.hpp, we have
>
>     template <typename T>
>     inline T sum(const std::vector<T>& xs) {
>       if (xs.size() == 0) return 0;
>       T sum(xs[0]);
>       for (size_t i = 1; i < xs.size(); ++i)
>         sum += xs[i];
>       return sum;
>     }
>

>
>     template <typename T>
>     inline T sum(const std::vector<T>& xs) {
>       return Eigen::Map< Eigen::Array<T, Dynamic, 1> >(&xs[0], xs.size(), 1).sum();
>     }
>
> And there are lots of C-style loops in Stan. But I really don't understand compilers or vectorization in the computer-science sense, so if I am wrong, can someone tell me why?

You're not wrong, most of those loops will be slower than Eigens code.  Sometimes compilers can be clever and use SIMD instructions automatically, but that is hard and doesn't always work depending on how the loop is written.  That said, I expect that the speedup of replacing every loop like that with an appropriate call to Eigen would be relatively small for most models because the overhead cost is going to be dominated by computations with vars which would be unaffected.

Cheers,
Marcus

Recycling means repeating the elements of a vector until they match the length of a longer vector. In other words, this is technically legal in R

> set.seed(12345)
> rnorm(6, mean = 0:2, sd = 4:5) # implicit recycling
[1]  2.342115  4.547330  1.562787 -2.267486  3.423550 -7.089780
> set.seed(12345)
> rnorm(6, mean = c(0:2, 0:2), sd = c(4:5, 4:5, 4:5)) # explicit recycling
[1]  2.342115  4.547330  1.562787 -2.267486  3.423550 -7.089780

where the colon means a sequence of integers from the left to the right. But I think implicit recycling is too dangerous for Stan, except recycling scalars to match the length of a vector / matrix / array.

messages.body_plain:
Option 0.  The way I would think about this is in terms
of coercing the various inputs to sequences,
throwing an exception if they don't match in
sequence size, and repeating the function as many times
as they do.

   scalar           -- recycle to max length
   std::vector      -- natural sequence
   Eigen column vec -- natural sequence
   Eigen row vec    -- natural sequence

This is what we have now

Option 1.  Extend this in the obvious way to matrices:

   Eigen matrix     -- column major order

This would match what we do now and also match how
Eigen defines operator()(int) for matrices.

If we do add them, I think it'll be simplest to just
define the natural sequentialization and allow
anything with matching sequence size.  This matches
Eigen's unary operator()(int) behavior.

I agree that recycling is a bad idea for anything
other than a scalar.  The only case I see it working
is recycling a row or column vector up to a matrix.
Or subarrays up to full arrays, like allowing
a CxD array to recycle up to an AxBxCxD array.
But that's starting to get awfully subtle.

Option 2.  The only other thing that seems simple is to require
all the types to match other than scalar.  But I
think everyone wants to allow 1D arrays, vectors
and row vectors to mix.

The major downside of this proposal is that you
could put in a 3 x 2 and a 2 x 3 matrix, and they'd
get converted to sequences as follows:

   a[1,1], a[2,1], a[3,1], a[2,1], a[2,2], a[3,2]

   b[1,1], b[2,1], b[1,2], b[2,2], b[1,3], b[2,3]

I can't imagine anywhere a user would do this and
it wouldn't be an error.

Option 3.  The in between spec would be to require the sizes
to all match, and if there are matrices and/or arrays,
their dimensions all have to match.

I'm OK with any of these options, including not extending
to matrices.

Also, what about 2D, 3D or greater arrays?

- Bob

>            if (xs.size() == 0) return 0;
>            T sum(xs[0]);
>            for (size_t i = 1; i < xs.size(); ++i)
>              sum += xs[i];
>            return sum;
>          }
>     |
>
>     which, if I understanding the packet-aligning business that Eigen does (and have the Map / Array syntax right) should be
>
>     |
>          template <typename T>
>          inline T sum(const std::vector<T>& xs) {
>            return Eigen::Map< Eigen::Array<T, Dynamic, 1> >(&xs[0], xs.size(), 1).sum();
>          }
>     |
>
>     And there are lots of C-style loops in Stan. But I really don't understand compilers or vectorization in the
>     computer-science sense, so if I am wrong, can someone tell me why?

Nobody does!  It's a rather empirical art from with a basis
partly in compilers and partly in CPU/bus/memory architecture.
The main point is that the CPU can do many operations in
parallel and it can prefetch data IF it can organize the data
into chunks properly and it can predict where it's going.

This book was really useful and I found it fun and it's
free online:

http://www.agner.org/optimize/optimizing_cpp.pdf

For example, in the Eigen-style code, you wind up constructing
new objects on the stack.  Their constructors aren't free,
but they're relatively pretty cheap and should be dwarfed by
the vectorization win for larger vectors.  Also, using two
loops can be worse than one or better -- sometimes the
compiler will itself do vectorization using the kind of stride
plus remainder business you saw in Eigen.

Partly it depends on context.

It also hugely changes over time as the relative speeds of
CPU, cache, memory and the availability of new instruction
sets, register organizations, etc. emerges.

I wasn't worrying too much about these issues because of
the following point from Marcus:

> You're not wrong, most of those loops will be slower than Eigens code.  Sometimes compilers can be clever and use SIMD
> instructions automatically, but that is hard and doesn't always work depending on how the loop is written.  That said, I
> expect that the speedup of replacing every loop like that with an appropriate call to Eigen would be relatively small
> for most models because the overhead cost is going to be dominated by computations with vars which would be unaffected.

This is why the unfolding of the auto-dif in the
matrix multiplies and in the probability function
code is such a big deal for speed.

The best way to get more speed in the other ops is to add
more analytic derivatives implemented in single chain()
functions.  And then pulling out a double-based
matrix or vector to send to Eigen.  At that point, all
the Eigen expression templates and vectorization should
help.

- Bob

From: Michael Collins <mcol...@csail.mit.edu>

Tamir Hazan is visiting on Tuesday - see the talk announcement below.

Cheers,
Mike

===============================================================
Title: Inference and Learning with Random Maximum A-Posteriori Perturbations

Speaker: Tamir Hazan, TTI Chicago

Time: 1.30-2.30pm Tuesday 16th October
Location: CS Building room 477

Abstract:
Learning and inference in complex models drives much of the research in machine learning applications, from computer
vision, natural language processing, to computational biology. The inference problem in such cases involves assessing
the weights of possible structures, whether objects, parsers, or molecular structures. Although it is often feasible to
only find the most likely or maximum a-posteriori (MAP) assignment rather than considering all possible assignment, MAP
inference is limited when there are other likely assignments. In a fully probabilistic treatment, all possible
alternative assignments are considered thus requiring summing over the assignments with their respective weights  which
is considerably harder (#P hard vs NP hard). The main surprising result of our work is that MAP inference (maximization)
can be used to approximate and bound the weighted counting. This leads us to a new approximate inference framework that
is based on MAP-statistics, thus does not depend on pseudo-probabilities, contrasting the current framework of Bethe
approximations which lacks statistical meaning. This approach excels in regimes where there are several but not
exponentially many prominent assignments. For example, this happens in cases where observations carry strong signals
(local evidence) but are also guided by strong consistency constraints (couplings).

Joint work with Tommi Jaakkola

Either the variate or parameters going to infinity will
result in -infinity log probabilities, right?  Those
will cause samples to be rejected.  Throwing an exception
just causes this to happen earlier rather than later.

We were also talking about CDFs.  On the linear scale,
those go to 0 or 1 outside the support of the PDF.

Mathematically, you can treat a PDF as a partial function
defined on its support that is non-zero everywhere it
is defined, or you can treat it as a total function that
has zero values.  Same for CDFs.

I personally have been advocating treating them as
partial functions, but everyone else seems to like
extending them.

> But if you happen to get such a value in Stan, it is going to overflow whatever is a function of it. And I
> thought overflow already caused a non-fatal exception. Maybe it depends on the policy or something?

It's not so much the exception being fatal or
non-fatal as the fact that our samplers catch
exceptison thrown by the model probability functions.

It will depend on policy, but that's not easily
configurable in RStan or Stan command line.  The
settings used there throw exceptions.

In C++, you can configure the static policy to instead
return -infinity (though I believe Daniel has them
all set to return NaN -- I think we'll fix that).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] checking values
messages.body_plain:
As I see it, there are two ways we can find ourselves considering a
state with log-probability of -inf:
1. Some (unconstrained) parameter is ±inf, in which case something
blew up in the simulation and we should probably consider a smaller
step size.
2. There are "holes" in the posterior that have 0 mass, in which case
decreasing the step size may help a little bit but not much (you've
got a very, very light tail) or might not help at all (you've got a
discontinuity).

(1) can happen quite naturally during adaptation. (2) suggests that
your model is making things more difficult than they need to be. I
believe we're already printing a "your posterior isn't continuous"
error during the initial step size adaptation (which tests whether
you're on the edge of a discontinuity), but maybe we should also be
printing a "your posterior has a hole in it" (or maybe something more
delicately worded) warning when we get -infs with finite parameters.

Matt

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] general optimization
messages.body_plain:
This is something I've been thinking about some lately, and at some
point will likely find a reason to implement in Stan.

I don't like pure MAP, for all of the reasons Andrew mentions and
probably some more that he hasn't mentioned. But I love maximum
marginal likelihood, which is what E-M usually implements (modulo
local optima). Ideally, I think I'd usually like to be doing MML on
some set of hyperparameters. Trouble is, you can't do E-M for lots of
hierarchical models, since the E step (wherein you compute p(z|y,θ))
is intractable. You can use variational inference, which can be
interpreted as an approximation to E-M, but it's pretty biased and can
be quite sensitive to local optima.

But you can also use MCMC within stochastic (generalized) E-M, if you
use an appropriately decaying step size or some other noise-robust
optimization framework. Which would be a pretty cool thing to support
in Stan. (Cf. my paper with David Mimno and David Blei on Sparse
Stochastic Inference for LDA.)

Matt

I have been working on (not pushed yet) implementing the stable distribution, which ironically can be numerically unstable.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_distribution

The density function cannot, in general, be written in closed form. However, Buckle

http://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=16815367252388880789&hl=en&as_sdt=0,33

showed that there exists a closed-form bivariate density with the same parameters, plus an auxiliary parameter vector of length N to form the second variate, such that its first marginal is a stable distribution. Buckle goes on to describe a MH / Gibbs algorithm that sounds like it would be much better and easier with HMC.

The tail fatness parameter, alpha, for a stable distribution is restricted to (0,2] except that it cannot be 1.0. For alpha values very near 1.0, numeric instability is to be expected.

I think there are two cases to be concerned about. One is that alpha in the population really is close to 1.0, in which case the stable distribution simplifies to a Cauchy (but the bivariate density seems not to simplify to anything). In that case, as long as the posterior mean is kind of close to 1.0, the user could probably just estimate a Cauchy model afterward. But the other case is that the alpha in the population is not really close to 1.0, but an alpha value very near 1.0 is accepted. In that case, we need to evaluate the log-posterior and gradient accurately enough to be able to get away from that point without having things blow up.

I can certainly push it without being able to using more than double precision. I am just saying it would hypothetically be nice to have.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
I'm down with that.

On Oct 15, 2012, at 5:47 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:

> This is something I've been thinking about some lately, and at some
> point will likely find a reason to implement in Stan.
>
> I don't like pure MAP, for all of the reasons Andrew mentions and
> probably some more that he hasn't mentioned. But I love maximum
> marginal likelihood, which is what E-M usually implements (modulo
> local optima). Ideally, I think I'd usually like to be doing MML on
> some set of hyperparameters. Trouble is, you can't do E-M for lots of
> hierarchical models, since the E step (wherein you compute p(z|y,θ))
> is intractable. You can use variational inference, which can be
> interpreted as an approximation to E-M, but it's pretty biased and can
> be quite sensitive to local optima.
>
> But you can also use MCMC within stochastic (generalized) E-M, if you
> use an appropriately decaying step size or some other noise-robust
> optimization framework. Which would be a pretty cool thing to support
> in Stan. (Cf. my paper with David Mimno and David Blei on Sparse
> Stochastic Inference for LDA.)
>
> Matt
>
> On Sun, Oct 14, 2012 at 8:10 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>> No, the big effort in lmer/blmer/etc is to compute the marginal likelihood (or approximate marginal likelihood) given the regression model.  The whole point is that you write the model and lmer etc figures out the integral.  It's done using a least squares computation, which probably isn't efficient and scalable approach.  If we really wanted to outdo bglmer using Stan, I don't think we'd do it by writing the marginal likelihood or approx marginal likelihood as a C++ function.
>> A
>>
>> On Oct 14, 2012, at 11:03 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>
>>>>>> What's the point of putting in posterior mode with Stan?
>>>>>
>>>>> It'd be a lot faster and more scalable.  Same reason
>>>>> you use (bg)lmer instead of BUGS.
>>>>
>>>> No.  Blmer computes (or approximates) the marginal posterior mode, not the joint posterior mode.  Much different.
>>>
>>> If we wrote a general optimizer, it wouldn't matter

>>> problem.  It'd be like Stan and optimize whatever

>>> of the debate about the utility of point estimates.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] asserts [was Re: "discontinuous posterior" warning cause]
messages.body_plain:
In general, assert() should be used to catch programmer error,
not to trap user errors.  It's then typical to turn them off
"in production".

1.  Calls to assert() in tests should be replaced with EXPECT_TRUE calls.

2. Calls to assert() elsewhere should be replaced with

   a)  runtime checks that throw exceptions if they are the
       result of user behavior, or

   b)  nothing if they are programmer error.

An alternative would be to leave the asserts for case 2b in
place and run with -DNDEBUG option.

I'll clean these up before the next release.  Any thoughts
on whether to just systematically remove all uses of assert()
or not?

- Bob

messages.subject: line numbers in error messages
messages.body_plain:
I think Bob mentioned that it would be good to have exceptions and other errors associate themselves with the line number in the code.

Apparently, this is easy with the __FILE__ and __LINE__ preprocessor macros, both of which seem to be supported by g++ and clang++; see

http://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/cpp/Standard-Predefined-Macros.html

or

goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/tmp$ cat test.cpp
#include<fstream>

int main() {
     fprintf (stderr, "Internal error: "
                      "look at "
                      "%s, line %d.\n",
              __FILE__, __LINE__);

    return 0;
}
goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/tmp$ clang++ test.cpp
goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/tmp$ ./a.out
Internal error: look at test.cpp, line 7.

Ben

messages.subject: seed in RStan (vs Stan)
messages.body_plain:
There are some difference between RStan and Stan in terms of how the seed is used. In RStan, I think taking a look at sampler_command in
https://code.google.com/p/stan/source/browse/rstan/rstan/inst/include/rstan/stan_fit.hpp
will help you.  I can remember there are at least tow differences:
1. initial values, in RStan, it is initialized once
2. reset seed before sampling. (Line 475)

So I think if you reset the seed in Stan before sampling, you might be able to get the same behavior.

--
Jiqiang

messages.subject: vectorized cdfs
messages.body_plain:
This email is mostly for Michael.

I've just added 3 parameter prob tests for cdfs. normal_cdf is the
only one that has been tested using it. Let me know what you think and
whether that's enough testing for cdfs.

See src/test/prob/distributions/univariate/continuous/normal_test.cpp

To implement one of these tests:
1) add a define for _CDF_
2) extend CumulativeTest. Define these functions:
    - void valid_values(vector<vector<double> >& parameters,
vector<double>& cdf)
      push back parameters and expected cdf values for the parameters specified.
    - void zero_values(vector<vector<double> >& parameters)
      push back parameter values that result in a cdf of zero
    - void one_values(vector<vector<double> >& parameters)
      push back parameter values that result in a cdf of one
    - void invalid_values(vector<size_t>& index, vector<double>& value)
      specific parameter values that should throw exceptions for the
default policy or errors with errno policy. This should match the one
defined for the log probability function
3) instantiate the tests. The instantiation looks something like:
INSTANTIATE_TYPED_TEST_CASE_P(ProbCumulativeNormal,
                              CumulativeTestFixture,
                              ProbCumulativeNormal);

The current tests are:
1) call_all_versions - calls the cdf function with and without a policy
2) check_valid - checks that the cdf function called with the
parameters specified in valid_values() returns the correct value
3) check_zero - checks that the cdf function called with the
parameters specified in zero_values() returns zero
4) check_one - checks that the cdf function called with the parameters
specified in one_values() returns one
5) check_invalid - checks that the parameter values throw exceptions
with no policy and errors with the errno_policy
6) vector_vector_vector - checks that the cdf value is correct with
vector parameters
7) vector_vector_double - checks that the cdf value is correct with
vector, vector, double
8) vector_double_vector - checks ... you get the point
9) vector_double_double
10) double_vector_vector,
11) double_vector_double,
12) double_double_vector,
13) invalid_different_vector_sizes - checks that the cdf function
throws an exception when vectors are mismatched in size.
14) matrix_matrix_matrix - checks that the cdf value is correct with
matrix<double, Dynamic, 1> parameters
15) matrix_matrix_double
16) matrix_double_matrix
17) matrix_double_double
18) double_matrix_matrix
19) double_matrix_double
20) double_double_matrix

The benefit of using the cdf fixture is that all of these tests get
run by defining a few parameters and values.

I'll put together the tests for agrad soon.

Daniel

messages.subject: limits, NaN, infinite parameters & variates
messages.body_plain:
Daniel and I were discussing what we want to do with
density and mass functions with limits.  (I'm setting
aside CDFs until we get the prob functions sorted.)

We're still thrashing without a decision.

My own feeling is that we should throw errors early
and often and that every case below other than those
marked OK should just throw a domain error.

There seemed to be substantial sentiment the other way,
but I still don't really understand why.   Maybe I confused
this with the CDF discussion, but I'd like to clarify now.
Maybe someone could be patient and re-explain to me why we
want to return -inf instead of raising errors.

Note that we've already given up trying to write a general
C++ probabability API as soon as we tied the density functions
to our auto-dif.  So I think the only issue is how this plays
into Stan.

Here's the set of possible behaviors for a few probability
functions.

A.  normal_log(y,mu,sigma);

    sigma    NaN        error
    sigma   -inf        error
    sigma   +inf        error [1]
    sigma    (-inf,0]   error [2]
    sigma    (0,+inf)   OK

    (y-mu)   NaN        error
    (y-mu)  -inf        -inf
    (y-mu)  +inf        -inf
    (y-mu)   fin        OK

[1]  Could limit sigma=inf case to be improper uniform
      and return an arbitrary constant

[2]  Could take sigma=0 to return +inf if y = mu
      and -inf otherwise

B.  beta_log(y,alpha,beta)

     alpha   NaN       error
     alpha   [-inf,0)  error
     alpha   0         error
     alpha   (0,inf)   OK
     alpha   inf       -inf [4]

     beta    (just like alpha)

     y       (0,1)     OK
     y       0         -inf [4]
     y       1         -inf [4]
     y       [-inf,0)  error
     y       (1,inf)   error

[4] alpha = inf, beta = finite, could lead to
     +inf probability for y=1 and -inf otherwise;
     similarly alpha=finite, beta=inf produces
     the reverse

C.  bernoulli_logit(y,alpha)

     alpha  NaN     error
     alpha  -inf    error [5]
     alpha  +inf    error [5]
     alpha  finite  OK

     y      < 0     error [6]
     y      > 1     error [6]
     y      {0,1}      OK

[5] If alpha = -inf, could return +inf for y = 1 and -inf for y = 0

[6] Could return -inf for y not in {0,1} on the principle that
     probability functions should be total for fixed valid params

Help!

- Bob

On Thursday, October 18, 2012 6:41:06 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Does the R code calculate the seed for subsequent chains
> the same way as the command line?  It should be, as that's
> the L'Ecuyer "parallel" seeding.

No, the default PRNG is Mersenne Twister. The L'Ecuyer (1999) algorithm is only an option. And even if they had that option chosen, the seed in stan() defaults to sample.int <http://sample.int>(.Machine$integer.max) rather than taking the seed from the state of the L'Ecuyer (1999) algorithm. (Which reminds me that I am still skeptical that the L'Ecuyer (1988) algorithm we are using from Boost has the properties of the L'Ecuyer (1999) algorithm).

Ben

I think the default behavior should be to choose
a random seed, not use -1.

Seeds are unsigned int in Stan (because they're
uint32_t in Boost).

See:

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_51_0/doc/html/boost/random/ecuyer1988.html

I don't think it matters how the random seed's
generated -- from R, from C++ according to the time,
whatever -- as long as it's available later to recreate.

 From stan/gm/command.hpp:

       unsigned int random_seed = 0;

       ...

       rng_t base_rng(random_seed);
       // (2**50 = 1T samples, 1000 chains)
       static boost::uintmax_t DISCARD_STRIDE = static_cast<boost::uintmax_t>(1) << 50;
       // DISCARD_STRIDE <<= 50;
       base_rng.discard(DISCARD_STRIDE * (chain_id - 1));

       typedef boost::ecuyer1988 rng_t;
       rng_t base_rng(random_seed);
       // (2**50 = 1T samples, 1000 chains)
       static boost::uintmax_t DISCARD_STRIDE = static_cast<boost::uintmax_t>(1) << 50;
       // DISCARD_STRIDE <<= 50;
       base_rng.discard(DISCARD_STRIDE * (chain_id - 1));

The discard skips ahead in the RNG sequence by the
specified number of draws.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] limits, NaN, infinite parameters & variates
messages.body_plain:
My general belief is that if the behaviour of a function can be consistently well defined then there's no need to throw an exception.  In most cases in stan there are no practical differences between the two cases for the domain of PDFs, but throwing exceptions reduces flexibility.  For instance, consider trying implement a mixture model where the components of the mixture have different supports.  E.G.,

p(x) = w_0 N(x|mu,sigma) + w_1 Beta(x|a,b) + w_3 Uniform(x|-1,0)

I'm not saying this is a common use case, but if a call to beta_log(x,a,b) throws an exception when x is outside of [0,1] then it would be hard (if not impossible) to implement it without a lot of extra work.  In contrast if beta_log returns -inf then it could be done in a relatively straightforward manner.

For distribution parameters I think exceptions make more sense because you could inadvertently get an improper prior in some cases and in many cases it's hard if not impossible to define things consistently.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] limits, NaN, infinite parameters & variates
messages.body_plain:
The reason we don't want to always throw an error is because infs can
happen naturally as a result of overflow during leapfrog steps. This
does indicate that the step size is too big, but that's something we
can and do deal with without dying.

I'm basically ok with Marcus's reasoning about not throwing domain
errors for random variables.

My feeling is that anywhere that a limit exists and makes sense we
should use it, since the typical case is that the simulation really
did "approach" 0 or infinity, and then got rounded off over the cliff.

The exception is where we'd get +inf density. We absolutely cannot
allow ourselves to get into such a state, because we'll never get out
again. I'm leaning towards saying we should actually return -inf when
we get a +inf. Which seems crazy, but it can be interpreted as
modifying the sampler to never transition to such states, which
actually preserves detailed balance (if not ergodicity).

A more principled reason is that in many cases you can justify it via
a change of variables to an unconstrained space. For example, consider
the gamma:
p(y) = exp{(a-1)*log(y) - b*y + a*log(b) - lgamma(a)}.
If you transform it so that x = log(y), then you get
p(x) = exp{a*x - b*exp(x) + a*log(b) - lgamma(a)}.
No more +infinities, and you get this limit behavior:
x=±inf (y=0 or inf): -inf.
a=0: -inf.
b=0: -inf.

My thoughts on specific distributions inline:

> A.  normal_log(y,mu,sigma);

sigma < 0: error.
sigma = 0, y-mu = 0: error or -inf.
sigma = 0, y-mu ≠ 0: -inf.
sigma = +inf: -inf.
y-mu = ±inf: -inf.

The 2nd case gives infinite density, which is bad.
The 3rd case can arise organically as a result of underflow, so we
should allow the sampler to recover gracefully from it.
The 4th and 5th cases can arise as a result of overflow, so we should
allow the sampler to recover gracefully from them.

> B.  beta_log(y,alpha,beta)

This is a tricky one. I say we go with the behavior on the
logit-transformed scale, i.e., think of x\in(-inf, inf) so that
p(x) = exp(alpha*log(x) - beta*log(1-x) - lgamma(alpha) - lgamma(beta)
+ lgamma(alpha + beta)).
Then things are clearer:
x=±inf (y=0 or 1): -inf
alpha or beta = 0: -inf
Errors if alpha or beta < 0.

> C.  bernoulli_logit(y,alpha)

This is a PMF, not a density, so numerical issues are less of a big
deal. Edge cases:
alpha = inf, y=1: 0
alpha = -inf, y=1: -inf
alpha = -inf, y=0: 0
alpha = inf, y=0: -inf

Matt

messages.subject: Simplify error handling?
messages.body_plain:
Bob and I were discussing this earlier today. Does anyone see a reason to keep the boost error handling framework in our library? So far, we've made allowed our distribution functions to have policy arguments, which is a bit if over-engineering. In order to implement the pattern provided by boost, we've also had to implement a lot of their base exception generating code, but with two template parameters instead of one. If we got rid of it, we would drop half the function signatures and we would have finer control of the error messages. If we ever need policies, we could reimplement them in the future.

Thoughts?

On Fri, Oct 19, 2012 at 8:31 AM, Marcus Brubaker
<marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Once we get the code in place to give model file line numbers with
> exceptions, we will also be able to easily check for lp__ == -inf and issue
> meaningful error messages without needing the *_log functions to throw
> exceptions.  We will still need to make that check due to potential
> underflow or programming issues with people directly manipulating lp__.

I don't think we shouldn't be throwing exceptions (line numbers or no)
just because lp__ == -inf, for the reasons I mentioned above. In my
opinion, we should only be throwing exceptions when we know the
problem is due to a modeling problem or due to something that could
only be due to a bug in Stan, not due to numerical issues. We really
need to be able to gracefully handle the scenario where a parameter
gets sufficiently large or small that lp__ overflows to -inf. Or, for
that matter, we'd like to potentially be able to support posteriors
with holes in them.

> The other possibility is to make the behaviour configurable, eg, with a
> template parameter.  Calls that happen as the result of a ~ statement could
> throw exceptions and all other calls return -inf for out of bounds
> behaviour.

I like this idea.

Matt

On 10/19/12 11:38 AM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
...

> I don't think we shouldn't be throwing exceptions (line numbers or no)
> just because lp__ == -inf, for the reasons I mentioned above. In my

> only be due to a bug in Stan, not due to numerical issues. We really
> need to be able to gracefully handle the scenario where a parameter
> gets sufficiently large or small that lp__ overflows to -inf.

By graceful here, do you just mean a normal (non-exception)
return from the function?

I keep thinking of the behavior in HMC, which is essentially
the same either way because we Metropolis reject -inf states.

We can already configure that at the Boost error level by having
domain errors not throw exceptions.

 > Or, for
> that matter, we'd like to potentially be able to support posteriors
> with holes in them.

You mean in the above sense of just having a non-exceptional
return?

>> The other possibility is to make the behaviour configurable, eg, with a
>> template parameter.  Calls that happen as the result of a ~ statement could
>> throw exceptions and all other calls return -inf for out of bounds
>> behaviour.
>
> I like this idea.

I think what Daniel may be suggesting in the way of more
configurability is to have a separate kind of Boost error
behavior, say "neg_inf_result", which we raise when there is
a -inf result.  The policy could then configure whether to
proceed or raise an exception before returning -inf.

All else being equal, I like configurability, too.  The main
issue is the growing complexity of the templates, particularly
how we have to hack pre-C++11 function template defaults.

(Speaking of which, one way to fix those would be to move
to static class functions rather than standalone functions.)

- Bob

n 10/19/12 2:24 PM, Matt Hoffman wrote:
> Sorry, I've been conflating exceptions and fatal errors. I'm ok with
> non-fatal exceptions, and defer to others' opinions on whether it's
> better to sound an alert when we hit -inf or not. My strong feelings

> were just about fatal exceptionsï¿½sorry for muddying the discussion.

Hang on!  You made me (and Daniel) think more deeply
about all of this.

I'd be happy going totally the other way with errors
and instead follow the std libs and

(a) return NaN when we get a NaN input

(b) return the appropriate finite, -inf, +inf or NaN depending
     on the input configs

(c) generalizing functions as much as possible [e.g., symmetrizing
     infinities on y and mu in normal(y|mu,sigma)].

As Daniel said, this is WAY simpler than what we have in
place now.  It'd cut out whole files full of error handling code
and "redundant" function signatures for default error handling.

We'd lose those "non-fatal warning (error: found NaN in ...)
and so on.  But those were just confusing people and making
them apprehensive about whether Stan was working.

Sampling output should be exactly the same (HMC/NUTS will reject
an -inf or NaN state).  I don't think there's an efficiency
issue because this is all in "error" handling.

- Bob

It's very configurable as long as we can implement
the Boost concept of a base random number generator.

The question I see is whether we need an RNG for
which it's efficient to advance the position in the
sequence.  This is what the one we're using lets you
do and I thought you (Ben) thought this was important.

So the issue would be how to generate a seed for
each chain using the Mersenne Twister or other RNG.

Is there some way to answer this question empirically?

Without forward simulation in generated quantities (not
implemented yet), we're bounded by:

   (dimensions + 1) * iterations * chains

Still, 2G isn't that much headroom.  50K iterations of
20K parameters would do it in a single chain.

But ecuyer1988 we're using is 2^61.

The citation is:

Efficient and Portable Combined Random Number Generators", Pierre L'Ecuyer, Communications of the ACM, Vol. 31, No. 6,
June 1988, pp. 742-749, 774

(I won't be able to read the paywalled ref until I
get back to Columbia.)

- Bob

On 10/18/12 10:14 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> I've not been able to find anything that comes out and enthusiastically says algorithms like his 1988 algorithm are okay
> for statistical computing. L'Ecuyer's most recent survey
>
> http://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=16324058590511781724&hl=en&as_sdt=0,33
>
> says that the period should be much bigger than the square of the number of pseudo-random numbers you need. I guess that
> depends on the number of parameters in our case. Is it conceivable that we would need 2 billion? In the last section, he
> says "Computer implementations that this author can suggest for the moment include ... " a few of his from the 1990s,
> the Mersenne-Twister ones, and a Fortran one.

> Ben

messages.body_plain:
On 10/18/12 9:08 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> My general belief is that if the behaviour of a function can be consistently well defined then there's no need to throw
> an exception.  In most cases in stan there are no practical differences between the two cases for the domain of PDFs,
> but throwing exceptions reduces flexibility.

Let's say it's differently abled flexibility-wise.

The exception makes it easier to report an edge case
likely arising due to an error.  In general, exceptions
are nicely flexible if you want to throw from multiple
functions and have a single catcher higher up.

In effect, our rejection for -inf or NaN values has the
same effect as the catch clause higher up, so the
exceptions aren't buying us much other than error reporting
and early termination (though I haven't looked into how.

The boundary return makes it easier to do arithmetic.
I think the case you give next is a good example!

Returning NaN or -inf should be at least as fast as
try/catch -- I started reading up on try/catch overhead
and quickly got in deeper than I wanted to.  I think
the answer is that if the other ops are expensive, try/catch
isn't that expensive if there's no catch, but it is some overhead
in tracking state.

> For instance, consider trying implement a mixture model where the
> components of the mixture have different supports.  E.G.,
>
> p(x) = w_0 N(x|mu,sigma) + w_1 Beta(x|a,b) + w_3 Uniform(x|-1,0)
>
> I'm not saying this is a common use case, but if a call to beta_log(x,a,b) throws an exception when x is outside of
> [0,1] then it would be hard (if not impossible) to implement it without a lot of extra work.  In contrast if beta_log
> returns -inf then it could be done in a relatively straightforward manner.

This is a good example of where you can go to infinity and
back again:

    log_sum_exp( log(w_0) + normal_log(x,mu,sigma),
                 log(w_1) + beta_log(x,a,b),
                 log(w_3) + uniform_log(x|-1,0) );

If any of the terms to log_sum_exp is -inf, it just gets
dropped, becase exp(-inf) = 0.

> For distribution parameters I think exceptions make more sense because you could inadvertently get an improper prior in
> some cases and in many cases it's hard if not impossible to define things consistently.

This is where Matt was arguing before we should have symmetry
between the errors thrown by:

    normal_log(y, mu, sigma)

    normal_log(0, y - mu, sigma);

    normal_log(0, (y - mu)/sigma, 1);

messages.subject: TRNG lib
messages.body_plain:
I looked at the TRNG PDF doc (it's a bit
out of date) and it shouldn't be a big deal to
swap it in for the ecuyer1988 version we're using
now.

The concepts we need to implement are on this page:

   http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_51_0/doc/html/boost_random/reference.html

Pretty much just some typedefs and

   operator()()

for generating RNGs and

   discard(uintmax_t)

for skipping ahead.

You can see an example here:

   http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_51_0/doc/html/boost/random/additive_combine_engine.html

We used the instantiation here:

   http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_51_0/doc/html/boost/random/ecuyer1988.html

- Bob

P.S.  I see now that TRNG used to be GPL, which would've
ruled it out before.  It's now BSD 3-clause, which is OK.

messages.subject: clang on Mac
messages.body_plain:
On Sunday, October 21, 2012 9:57:26 AM UTC-4, Jiqiang Guo wrote:
> 2. clang might not work well on old Mac say even Snow Leopard for rstan (ie, old version in Xcode), I will report some details later.

Perhaps I spoke too soon, but it raises a different question that I don't know enough about Macs to answer for sure.

I would speculate that the average Mac user of (R)Stan is better off with a recent version of clang than with g++-4.2.x. We think we think that g++ generates somewhat faster code than clang++ does, but I don't know what we have thoroughly benchmarked that and I somewhat doubt that g++-4.2.x generates faster code than clang++ 3.x. We still have to support g++-4.2.x because that is what CRAN uses for a Mac, but I don't think that implies we should be recommending people use g++-4.2.x on a Mac.

I only know of two potential problems. One is that maybe clang is difficult to install on some Macs. Is it not a simple matter of going to

http://llvm.org/releases/download.html

and downloading the most recent version that works on whatever cat you have? Maybe you have to put in on your $PATH? The other problem is that clang has had compatibility problems with Rcpp in the past. But Dirk claims to have hopefully resolved them in the latest version:

http://dirk.eddelbuettel.com/blog/2012/10/14#rcpp_0.9.15

So, am I overlooking something?

Ben

> We could also incorporate the process ID in the seeding or, if you want to be really clever, read some data from /dev/random to seed things.

/dev/random doesn't work on Windows, although inside R it is fairly easy to get a seed from www.random.org <http://www.random.org> with the random package.

Maybe we could incorporate the process ID if chain_id is not set. But I think the best route is "same seed, different chain_id, modern PRNG".

Ben

On Sun, Oct 21, 2012 at 11:04 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

> On Sunday, October 21, 2012 10:28:51 PM UTC-4, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> > We could also incorporate the process ID in the seeding or, if you want to be really clever, read some data from /dev/random to seed things.
>
> /dev/random doesn't work on Windows, although inside R it is fairly easy to get a seed from www.random.org <http://www.random.org> with the random package.

>From R it might make sense to get a random draw from the R PRNG to seed the Stan PRNG.  This has the upside that the user gets the expected behaviour in their code by storing/setting the R PRNG state and, unless they want to, never need to know or worry about a separate PRNG inside stan.

>
> Maybe we could incorporate the process ID if chain_id is not set. But I think the best route is "same seed, different chain_id, modern PRNG".

I was only suggesting using the PID when the seed wasn't specified to avoid starting multiple chains with the same seed by accident.  For instance, someone may not use the chain id (I mean, right now it's effect is purely cosmetic) and instead just launch N copies of command line stan with different out files.  If all (or even a few) of them got the same seed this would be bad.

Cheers,
Marcus

At this point, it is easier to benchmark rstan. I made a rstan package from master after setting g++ in $HOME/.R/Makevars and did

example(stan_demo)

  execute <- system.time(fit <- stan_demo(i, fit = fit, seed = 12345, refresh = -1))

  return(rbind(compile, execute))
}

results <- mclapply(1:length(model_names), mc.cores = 4L, FUN = bench,
                    mc.preschedule = FALSE)

names(results) <- model_names

On Monday, October 22, 2012 6:22:27 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Monday, October 22, 2012 6:03:50 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > Anyone else have anything they want to get in
> > for this release?
>
> I'd like to try to make the manual for 1.0.3 diff-able relative to 1.0.2, but I think I am almost ready to do that.

No one really expressed a strong opinion as to whether this was a good idea. So, I am going to push some changes soon unless someone speaks up.

I do something like ./diff.sh v1.0.2 HEAD and then make manual, which causes the manual to
Display (most) lines that have been added or changed in green text
Adds one "comment note" per modified page to the margin of the PDF which should be visible in Adobe products and Preview
Adds a "List of Corrections" page at the very end with clickable links and page references to the aforementioned "comment notes"
Limitations:
Not every change is processed for various reasons
If there is a change inside a Verbatim environment, the macros are interpreted verbatim rather than as macros and hence look messed up. See for example the second change on page 7 of the attachment. This problem can be solved by using the alltt environment rather than the Verbatim environment, which typesets things like the Verbatim environment but interprets macros. The cost of this is that we would have to escape stuff in the alltt environment, such as
parameters { # needs to be \{
  real theta; \\ comment # needs to be \\\\ comment
} # needs to be \}

We only need to make the transition from Verbatim to alltt for places where the manual changes relative to the last release, so it is not a huge deal. But I am going to wait to hear something before I start pushing changes like that.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] assigning to a column of a matrix
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] assigning to a column of a matrix
messages.body_plain:
On 10/22/12 7:04 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> Is this supposed to be unsupported?

It matches the doc, if that's what you mean.

There's a full BNF for Stan in the manual.  The only
thing allowable on the left-hand side of an assignment
statement is a variable + optional indices.

> |
>          col(slopes,j) <- if_else(j - 1, beta[j-1], 0.0) + col(slopes_error,j);
>          ^-- here

The reason it's not an easy fix is that the function
col() returns a value, not a reference.

We could, perhaps, generalize return types within
Stan to allow references and then allow more general
lvalues on the LHS of <-.  If we do that, we'd have to
be careful in the manual to separate functions that
return lvalues from functions that return values.

It's trickier with something like diag(m) where m is
a matrix.  To get that to work, we'd either need to return
views with all the headaches that entails with templates
or convert all of our matrices to be matrices of references
instead of matrices of values, which I don't think is a good
idea for performance.

I was thinking we'd solve this problem eventually by
moving the colon notation for indices, where we could
write:

  slopes[j,:] <- ...

- Bob

messages.subject: LaTeX diffs (for 1.0.3)
messages.body_plain:
If you feel strongly about it, go right ahead.
I do have some caveats below.

On 10/23/12 12:53 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Monday, October 22, 2012 6:22:27 PM UTC-4, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>
>     On Monday, October 22, 2012 6:03:50 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>         Anyone else have anything they want to get in
>         for this release?
>
>
>     I'd like to try to make the manual for 1.0.3 diff-able relative to 1.0.2, but I think I am almost ready to do that.
>
>
> No one really expressed a strong opinion as to whether this was a good idea.

I don't think it's hugely important, but that shouldn't stop
anyone from doing something they think is important, which
is why I wasn't more decisive in terms of what I thought we
should do before.

If you do want to leave it up to me or take a vote, I'd say
no -- keep things as simple as possible build-wise.

> So, I am going to push some changes soon
> unless someone speaks up.

I have a strong preference for simplicity and direct
connection between my LaTeX and the output.   I've been
burned too many times by fancy pre- and post-processing
that only partly works.

So I have a very strong preference that any manual
with diffs be SEPARATE from the main manual we
distribute.   If you do that, I'm happy with whatever
the actual task does and whatever the output is.

I don't want to have to put any effort into maintaining it
myself.  (That's why, by the way, we still don't have a fancier
web page -- if someone wants to take over converting what we
have to use some content-generation tools AND wants to maintain
it in the future, go right ahead.)

> I do something like ./diff.sh v1.0.2 HEAD and then make manual, which causes the manual to
>

>   * Display (most) lines that have been added or changed in green text
>   * Adds one "comment note" per modified page to the margin of the PDF which should be visible in Adobe products and Preview
>   * Adds a "List of Corrections" page at the very end with clickable links and page references to the aforementioned
>     "comment notes"
>
> Limitations:
>
>   * Not every change is processed for various reasons
>   * If there is a change inside a Verbatim environment, the macros are interpreted verbatim rather than as macros and

>     hence look messed up. See for example the second change on page 7 of the attachment. This problem can be solved by
>     using the alltt environment rather than the Verbatim environment, which typesets things like the Verbatim
>     environment but interprets macros. The cost of this is that we would have to escape stuff in the alltt environment,
>     such as

> parameters { # needs to be \{
>    real theta; \\ comment # needs to be \\\\ comment
> } # needs to be \}
> |
>
> We only need to make the transition from Verbatim to alltt for places where the manual changes relative to the last
> release, so it is not a huge deal. But I am going to wait to hear something before I start pushing changes like that.

Will alltt handle ~ inline properly (that is, not
make it a superscript and put it in the right font)?

- Bob

wallet!   For more of a taste:

   Q:  How are a violists fingers like lightning?

horn jokes around, or if this was purely one way.  There
are lots of viola jokes,

and a few horn jokes:

    http://www.mit.edu/~jcb/jokes/#horn

For instance, here's one he'd have liked, despite being
a Dodge man:

    Q:  What is the difference between a french horn section and a '57 Chevy?
    A:  You can tune a '57 Chevy.

messages.subject: pushed truncation tests in stanc
messages.body_plain:
Daniel and I put our heads together and I added
some tests to the parser and code generator so
that stanc will now flag and report errors in
attempting to use truncation for densities for
which we don't have a CDF or attempt to use truncation
with vectorization, which we don't support (yet).

Longer-term, for efficiency and to make vectorization
simpler, we'll probably just roll truncation into the
probabilty functions, so we'd have functions that look
like:

   normal_log(y,mu,sigma);
   normal_lb_log(y,mu,sigma,L);
   normal_ub_log(y,mu,sigma,H);
   normal_lub_log(y,mu,sigma,L,H);

or with something longer if Andrew thinks "lb", "ub"
and "lub" are tacky and he can come up with better
alternatives :-)

- Bob

messages.subject: v1.0.3 release note help?
messages.body_plain:
We're pretty much set for the release.  I'm going to
spend the next couple of hours making some updates,
upload the new manual and Stan tarball, and then turn
it over to Jiqiang for the RStan release.

When RStan goes out, we need to update the web pages,
too, which I've updated on git, but haven't pushed
to the web server.

Here's what I have so far.  There must be a lot
of things I'm missing.  As far as I know, we're not
doing a similar thing for RStan, but I'd like to point
out that we can now parallelize (at least on Linux and
Mac).

v 1.0.3 Release Notes
======================================================================
Bug Fixes:
  -- error output in stanc now directed to standard error
  -- catching all exceptions thrown in stanc to prevent core dumps
  -- parser now accepts variable names starting with "int" and "real"
     in first assignment after declaration
  -- now catching unknown truncation cdfs and vectorizations in stanc
New Features:
  -- mdivide_left_tri_low, mdivide_right_tri_low functions
  -- all univariate continuous densities vectorized
  -- better error checking for transforms
  -- new error return type in stanc for invalid arguments
  -- lower and upper bounds for vectors, row vectors, and matrices
Manual Additions:
  -- example of defining new distribution with parameters

- Bob
